name: Street Custom 'Trash Armor' Improvised Body Protection
product_name: Street Custom 'Trash Armor' Improvised Body Protection
description: Body armor improvised from whatever materials are available — layers of duct tape and phone books over vital areas, road sign metal cut into chest plates, layers of ceramic tile taped together, or vehicle floor mats worn as vests. Trash Armor is the protective equipment of people who cannot afford real armor, and its effectiveness varies from surprisingly adequate (layered ceramics can stop handgun rounds) to dangerously inadequate (duct tape and cardboard). The cultural significance of Trash Armor in Tier 1 is that wearing it acknowledges a specific reality: your life is dangerous enough to need armor, and you are poor enough that this is the best you can do.

specifications.protection: Variable — ranges from NIJ Level I to nothing useful
specifications.info: road signs; phone books; floor mats

story_hooks: A Tier 1 resident survived a shooting because their Trash Armor — six layers of ceramic floor tile — stopped a handgun round. The incident has become a viral moment that highlights the absurd ingenuity of survival in the lower tiers.

A Trash Armor design using a specific combination of layered materials has been tested and found to outperform some commercial body armor at 1/100th the cost — the design is spreading and corporate armor manufacturers are not happy.

physical_description.visual_profile: Asymmetrical, crude torso protection assembled from salvaged materials. Multiple disparate layers visible — jagged metal plates wired or taped over ceramic tile sections, all held together with industrial duct tape in grey and silver. The construction looks deliberately rough, almost punk-aesthetic in its refusal of finished appearance.
physical_description.dimensions: Torso-covering vest form factor, approximately 60cm wide × 50cm tall, extending from shoulders to waist
physical_description.weight_description: Heavy depending on build — ceramic-tile variants weigh 4-8kg and require shoulder support; lighter duct-tape versions around 2-3kg but less protective
physical_description.primary_material: Composite — ceramic tile sections, cut road sign metal (steel/aluminum), salvaged vehicle floor mats (rubber, plastic composites), reinforced with industrial duct tape and wire binding
physical_description.finish: Raw, unfinished. Weathered metal with rust patina, chipped white ceramic tile edges, torn grey duct tape with visible seams, frayed rubber mat edges. No polish or refinement.
physical_description.color_scheme: Monochromatic greys and silvers — rust-stained metal, grey duct tape, off-white ceramic tile, charcoal rubber. Occasional faded road sign paint (yellows, reds) showing through gaps
physical_description.interface_elements: None — completely passive. Leather or synthetic straps for securing; visible wire loops or D-rings for attachment points. No electronics, displays, or interactive elements.
distinctive_features: Visible layering with gaps showing interior construction
Multiple tape seams creating geometric segmentation
Protruding wire frame visible at edges holding plates together
Uneven surface with tiles and metal at different depths
Dried mud or street grime in seams
Worn rope or paracord binding at shoulders
Faded reflective road-sign segments catching light
physical_description.manufacturer_markings: None — street custom means no branding. Occasionally street artist tags or names spray-painted on duct tape, personal modifications only
physical_description.condition_typical: Visibly battle-worn. Duct tape peeling at edges, visible impact dents in metal and tile, fresh tears alongside old patches. Looks perpetually one bad fight away from catastrophic failure
